Any three characteristics, each with its reason:

  • Variable oxidation states — 4s and 3d electrons are close in energy, so different numbers can be lost/shared.
  • Coloured compounds — ligands split the d orbitals; electrons absorb visible light in d–d transitions.
  • Form complex ions — empty d orbitals accept electron pairs from ligands.
  • Catalytic activity — can change oxidation state easily / form complexes with reactants.

(i) A ligand is a molecule or anion with a lone pair that forms a coordination (dative) bond to a central metal atom or ion.

(ii) A Lewis acid–base reaction: H2O is the Lewis base (electron-pair donor) and Fe2+ is the Lewis acid (electron-pair acceptor). Both points needed.

(iii) Ligands split the d orbitals into two sets of different energy, and electron transitions between them absorb visible light. Different ligands (H2O vs CN−) split the d orbitals by different amounts, so different wavelengths are absorbed and the complexes have different colours.

(i) Across the period electrons are added to the same main energy level (similar shielding), while nuclear charge (number of protons) increases, so the outer electrons are held more strongly.

(ii) Mg is 3s2, Al is 3s23p1. The 3p electron in Al is in a higher-energy sublevel (and partly shielded by 3s), so it is easier to remove.

(iii) P is 3p3, with each p electron unpaired in separate orbitals; S is 3p4, with one pair of electrons in the same orbital. Repulsion between the paired electrons makes one easier to remove, so S has a lower IE.

2. The same nuclear charge (3+) now attracts fewer electrons, so the effective nuclear charge per electron is greater and the remaining electrons are pulled closer (less repulsion).

(i) IE(K) < IE(Na): K's outer electron is in n = 4, further from the nucleus and more shielded [1]. IE(K) is much less than IE(Ar) [1]: Ar's outer electrons are in n = 3, closer to the nucleus, and Ar has a much higher nuclear charge than Na (same shell), so its electrons are held far more tightly than K's single 4s electron [1].

(ii) Na and Mg have outer electrons in the same shell (n = 3) [1]; Mg has greater nuclear charge (12 vs 11 protons) [1] with similar shielding, so electrons are pulled closer → Mg has smaller atomic radius [1] and higher first IE [1].

(iii) Na's second electron comes from n = 2 (closer, much less shielded), but Mg's second electron comes from n = 3 [1]; so 2nd IE of Na is much higher than that of Mg [1].
